We define three contamination types with increasing severity, namely Benchmark Metadata Leakage, Question-Context Leakage, and Explicit Answer Leakage, and develop detection algorithms to identify them and quantify their impact on agent performance. Evaluating modern deep research agents on six public benchmarks, we find that STC is widespread and can inflate performance by up to 4%. Our findings show that existing evaluations may overestimate true reasoning ability. We therefore advocate contamination-aware practices, including isolated sandboxes, transparent search trajectories, and controlled benchmark access.
tldr: This paper studies how deep research agents that search the web during inference can be contaminated by benchmark metadata, question context, or answers, inflating performance by up to 4%.
motivation: Public benchmarks are widely used to evaluate LLM reasoning, but deep research agents that retrieve external information during inference may inadvertently access benchmark data, leading to overestimated performance.
method: The authors define three types of search-time contamination (metadata leakage, question-context leakage, explicit answer leakage) and develop detection algorithms to identify them. They evaluate modern deep research agents on six public benchmarks.
result: Search-time contamination is widespread and can inflate performance by up to 4%, indicating that existing evaluations may overestimate true reasoning ability.
conclusion: The findings advocate for contamination-aware evaluation practices such as isolated sandboxes, transparent search trajectories, and controlled benchmark access.

title: From Attack Simulation To Siem Rule: Deterministic Detection-as-Code Synthesis With Probe-Level Traceability
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05252v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Security teams routinely simulate attacks against their own systems to check whether their monitoring would catch a real intruder. These Breach-and-Attack-Simulation (BAS) tools surface findings, but the security information and event management (SIEM) systems that watch production need detection rules -- and today a human bridges that gap by hand, reading each finding and writing the corresponding Sigma rule (a vendor-neutral detection format). We show this translation can be partially automated when probes are drawn from a locked corpus, so each finding carries a stable identifier back to the originating probe. We describe a deterministic synthesis function that maps each finding to a starter Sigma rule through a small template library (N=23, indexed by categories from the OWASP LLM and Web Top 10), with a back-reference to the originating finding and its MITRE ATT&CK technique. On two locked corpora (17-probe LLM, 23-probe Web), every bypassed-probe finding yields a starter rule, and all 17/17 emitted rules parse and convert to Splunk and Elasticsearch backends. Replayed through a live OpenSearch SIEM, the LLM rules fire on 30% of a held-out AdvBench subset and 14% of HarmBench at 7.7% false positives on a benign baseline; the Web side is validated structurally, not against a held-out attack set. The contribution is a verifiable, byte-stable path from BAS finding to operator-deployable starter rule, re-derivable from the published corpus and template library alone -- trading the breadth of LLM-generative methods for exact reproducibility and a typed traceback from any fired alert to the originating probe.
tldr: This paper presents a deterministic method to convert BAS probe findings into SIEM detection rules (Sigma rules) with full traceability, focusing on cybersecurity automation.
motivation: Security teams need to translate attack simulation findings into detection rules, a manual process that is slow and error-prone.
method: The authors design a template library (N=23) indexed by OWASP categories and a deterministic synthesis function that maps each finding to a starter Sigma rule with back-references to the probe and MITRE ATT&CK technique.
result: On two locked corpora (17-probe LLM, 23-probe Web), all bypassed-probe findings yield starter rules; LLM rules fire on 30% of AdvBench and 14% of HarmBench with 7.7% false positives.
conclusion: The approach provides a verifiable, reproducible path from BAS findings to deployable detection rules, trading breadth for exact reproducibility and traceability.

title: Should Demand Models Incorporate Competitor Prices? Oblivious Learning And Algorithmic Collusion
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05363v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On a platform with many sellers, should a pricing algorithm explicitly model competitors' prices when learning demand? Classical learning arguments suggest an affirmative answer: ignoring competitors induces model misspecification and inefficiency. In contrast, recent work on algorithmic collusion suggests that strategic obliviousness -- deliberately ignoring competitor prices -- may facilitate collusive outcomes and improve profits. We study this modeling choice in a stylized competitive market with unknown noisy demand, in which multiple sellers repeatedly set prices and estimate demand via iterated least squares, and either incorporate competitors' prices into their demand models (informed) or ignore them (oblivious). We first show that, relative to a monopolist, an oblivious seller in a competitive market must explore more aggressively to compensate for the loss of dynamic competitor information. Building on this insight, we characterize market dynamics when all sellers are oblivious and show that prices converge to the competitive outcome under sufficient exploration, while a continuum of pseudo-equilibria arises when exploration decays. Analyzing the resulting price trajectories, we uncover an excursion phenomenon that gives rise to transient collusive patterns that dissipate as learning progresses. In markets with both oblivious and informed sellers, the informed strictly out-earn the oblivious. Read as a strategy game, the modeling choice has a unique Nash equilibrium: the all-informed market, in which prices converge to the competitive outcome efficiently. Overall, our results indicate that collusive patterns are not robust and are not sustained by oblivious modeling; therefore, incorporating competitor information, together with sufficient price exploration, remains a reliable strategy for sellers in competitive markets.
tldr: This paper studies whether pricing algorithms should model competitor prices, finding that oblivious learning can lead to transient collusive patterns but informed learning is the unique Nash equilibrium and yields competitive outcomes.
motivation: To resolve the tension between classical learning arguments (which favor incorporating competitor prices) and recent work on algorithmic collusion (which suggests obliviousness may facilitate collusion).
method: The authors model a competitive market with multiple sellers using iterated least squares to estimate demand, comparing oblivious sellers (who ignore competitor prices) with informed sellers (who incorporate them). They analyze market dynamics, convergence, and pseudo-equilibria.
result: Oblivious sellers must explore more aggressively; prices converge to competitive outcomes under sufficient exploration, but transient collusive patterns appear when exploration decays. Informed sellers outperform oblivious ones, and the all-informed market is the unique Nash equilibrium.
conclusion: Collusive patterns from oblivious learning are not robust; incorporating competitor information with sufficient exploration is a reliable strategy for sellers.

title: A Formal Framework For The Economic Security Of DeFi Compositions
authors: Massimo Bartoletti, Riccado Marchesin, Roberto Zunino
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05418v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decentralized Finance (DeFi) services are usually constructed by composing a variety of smart contracts. While composability is a key driver of the success of DeFi, it also creates security risks: adversaries may exploit interactions between newly deployed contracts and the pre-existing ones to inflict economic losses. We introduce MEV non-interference, a formal security notion for DeFi composability requiring that the maximal extractable value from a set of newly deployed contracts is not increased by interactions with the existing blockchain state. To support this notion, we define local MEV, a novel measure of economic attacks that focusses on the loss of a given set of victim contracts. We study two adversarial models, with bounded and unbounded wealth, and establish sufficient conditions and locality principles that enable modular reasoning about secure composability. We apply the framework to representative DeFi compositions, including exchanges, AMMs, options, lending pools, routers, and arbitrage contracts, showing how it distinguishes secure compositions from vulnerable ones. Our results provide a formal foundation for reasoning about the economic security of DeFi compositions.
tldr: This paper introduces a formal framework for economic security of DeFi compositions, focusing on MEV non-interference and local MEV.
motivation: DeFi composability creates security risks where adversaries exploit interactions between contracts to cause economic losses.
method: The authors define MEV non-interference and local MEV, study adversarial models with bounded/unbounded wealth, and establish sufficient conditions for secure composability.
result: The framework distinguishes secure from vulnerable DeFi compositions, applied to exchanges, AMMs, options, lending pools, routers, and arbitrage contracts.
conclusion: Provides a formal foundation for reasoning about economic security of DeFi compositions, enabling modular analysis.

title: Policy-Compliant Cloud Storage Systems
authors: Dimitrios Stavrakakis, Masanori Misono, Julian Pritzi, Harshavardhan Unnibhavi, Nuno Santos, Pramod Bhatotia
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05423v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Privacy regulations such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) impose strict requirements on how personal data is stored, processed, and audited. While key-value stores (KVS) are widely used in latency-sensitive applications, their simple data model and untrusted cloud deployment environments make GDPR compliance particularly challenging. Existing approaches require invasive code modifications, impose high performance overheads, or overlook the integrity of compliance mechanisms themselves. This paper presents GDPRuler, a trusted middleware system that enables verifiable GDPR compliance for KVS on untrusted clouds without modifying their codebase. GDPRuler deploys a trusted GDPR monitor inside a Confidential Virtual Machine (CVM), which enforces GDPR policies, manages compliance metadata, and maintains tamper-evident audit logs. A declarative policy language translates core GDPR obligations into enforceable runtime rules. To ensure efficiency, GDPRuler encodes metadata compactly within KV records, builds dedicated metadata indexes for GDPR-specific queries, and logs only compliance-relevant events in a space-efficient format. We implement GDPRuler as a transparent proxy for unmodified Redis and RocksDB deployments. Evaluation with YCSB and GDPR-inspired workloads shows that GDPRuler enforces core compliance guarantees with low overheads: GDPRuler achieves ~61% of native KVS throughput with the CVM environment contributing 28%-32% of it, metadata storage overhead remains below 20%, and GDPR queries benefit from 13-182x speedup through metadata indexing. By embedding verifiable policy enforcement into a trusted middleware layer, GDPRuler offers a practical path toward GDPR-compliant KVS on untrusted cloud infrastructures.
tldr: GDPRuler is a trusted middleware system that enables verifiable GDPR compliance for key-value stores on untrusted clouds without modifying their codebase.
motivation: Privacy regulations like GDPR impose strict requirements on data storage and processing, but existing approaches for key-value stores require invasive code changes, have high overhead, or overlook integrity of compliance mechanisms.
method: GDPRuler deploys a trusted GDPR monitor inside a Confidential Virtual Machine (CVM) to enforce policies, manage metadata, and maintain tamper-evident audit logs, using a declarative policy language and compact metadata encoding.
result: GDPRuler achieves ~61% of native KVS throughput with CVM overhead of 28-32%, metadata storage below 20%, and 13-182x speedup for GDPR queries via indexing.
conclusion: GDPRuler provides a practical path toward GDPR-compliant KVS on untrusted clouds by embedding verifiable policy enforcement into a trusted middleware layer.

title: Cress: Quantifying Vulnerabilities Of Attack Scenarios In Hardware Reverse Engineering
authors: Alexander Hepp, Matthias Ludwig, Michaela Brunner, Johanna Baehr, Georg Sigl
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05459v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The safety, security, and reliability of microelectronic systems depend on a trustworthy, secured supply chain and design flow. Globally distributed supply chains or unintentional design weaknesses leave the door open for attacks on the hardware level. These scenarios encompass counterfeiting, hardware trojans, or on-device attacks. For these, hardware reverse engineering (RE) results play a pivotal role. The ongoing publication of new RE-involved attacks motivated the development of the common RE scoring system (CRESS). The system enables a general classification of RE-involved scenarios for a common, consistent rating. In this work, the originally qualitative system is extended to a quantitative system. We performed an extensive interview study with experts in the field. The interview results allowed us to derive weights that measure the severity of different RE-involved attack categories. The weights form an equation that quantifies scenarios, resulting in the severity-indicating CRESS score. The score enables the coherent rating of novel scenarios, renders them comparable, and supports the development of effective countermeasures. To showcase the effectiveness of the quantitative CRESS Score, six selected case studies are rated qualitatively and quantitatively. The CRESS Score proves to be significantly more expressive than the industry-standard Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS).
tldr: This paper introduces a quantitative scoring system (CRESS) for hardware reverse engineering attack scenarios, unrelated to quantum computing or the user's research interests.
motivation: Hardware reverse engineering attacks pose security risks, and existing scoring systems like CVSS are inadequate for RE-involved scenarios.
method: The authors conducted an expert interview study to derive weights for attack categories, then formulated a quantitative equation to compute a CRESS score.
result: The CRESS score provides a more expressive and comparable rating of RE-involved attack scenarios than CVSS, demonstrated through six case studies.
conclusion: CRESS enables consistent severity assessment and supports development of countermeasures for hardware reverse engineering attacks.

title: Shields: Automating Os Hardening With Iterative Multi-Agent Remediation
authors: Andrew Hamara, Dwight Horne, Aldehir Rojas, Timothy Kurniawan, Sophie Lamothe, Vishal Suresh, Nicholas Turoci, Lawrence Wong
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05476v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Security misconfigurations remain a leading cause of OS-level compromise, and manually keeping systems compliant with standards like Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) Security Technical Implementation Guides (STIGs) is a tedious and expensive process. Existing compliance automation tools can reduce some of this burden, but they depend on static, pre-written corrective actions. In this paper, we introduce SHIELDS, a multi-agent system that uses large language models (LLMs) to approach OS hardening as an iterative, feedback-driven process. Instead of applying fixed remediations, SHIELDS continuously proposes fixes and refines them based on feedback from target system execution and validation scans. We evaluate the system across multiple virtual machine configurations using six contemporary LLMs ranging from 20B to 400B parameters, and find that SHIELDS successfully remediates up to 73% of scan findings. Our results also suggest that success in this setting depends less on model size (parameter count) than on effective tool use and information gathering, paving a practical path toward reducing the burden of security compliance in environments where compute is limited or security and privacy needs drive local model use.
tldr: SHIELDS is a multi-agent LLM system that automates OS hardening by iteratively proposing and refining fixes based on feedback from compliance scans.
motivation: Manual OS hardening against standards like DISA STIGs is tedious and expensive; existing automation tools rely on static, pre-written fixes that may not adapt to diverse configurations.
method: The system uses multiple LLM agents to propose remediation actions, execute them on target VMs, receive feedback from validation scans, and iteratively refine the fixes until compliance is achieved.
result: SHIELDS successfully remediated up to 73% of scan findings across various VM configurations using LLMs from 20B to 400B parameters; success depended more on tool use and information gathering than on model size.
conclusion: LLM-driven iterative remediation can reduce the burden of security compliance, especially in resource-constrained or privacy-sensitive environments, and suggests that effective agent design matters more than raw model scale.

title: Bitcoin After Block Rewards
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05503v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bitcoin's block reward is scheduled to decline to zero, raising concerns about whether the network can remain secure once miners rely solely on transaction fees. This paper seeks to identify the conditions under which large-scale and persistent deviation from honest mining can arise. We analyze and compare the payoffs of honest and deviating miners in a sequential decision model, and identify a deviation threshold [MATH] at which honest mining ceases to be privately optimal. Around the 2024 Bitcoin halving, we show that current mining behavior does not exhibit large-scale or structural deviation. However, when the block reward is removed, the [MATH] criterion implies that deviation can arise even with a very small fraction of transaction fees. Finally, we evaluate three protocol-level mechanisms: Base Fee, Fee Floor, and an adaptive maximum block size rule, and show that their combination raises the deviation threshold and mitigates incentive breakdown in a fee-only regime. These results provide a practical benchmark for assessing Bitcoin's security as block rewards disappear.
tldr: This paper analyzes Bitcoin's security after block rewards end, focusing on miner incentives and protocol mechanisms.
motivation: Bitcoin's block reward is scheduled to decline to zero, raising concerns about network security when miners rely solely on transaction fees.
method: The authors use a sequential decision model to compare payoffs of honest and deviating miners, identifying a deviation threshold.
result: Around the 2024 halving, no large-scale deviation is observed, but after block rewards end, deviation can arise even with a small fraction of transaction fees. A combination of Base Fee, Fee Floor, and adaptive max block size raises the deviation threshold.
conclusion: The proposed protocol mechanisms can mitigate incentive breakdown in a fee-only regime, providing a benchmark for Bitcoin's security as block rewards disappear.

title: Polynomial-time Satisfiability For A Special Case Of Positive$\wedge$Negative
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05512v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A Boolean function in CNF format is of type Positive[MATH]Negative} if each clause C is either positive (i.e. all literals of C are positive) or negative (i.e. all literals of C are negative). As is well known, deciding the satisfiability of such CNFs is NP-complete. We say that a CNF is of type DisjointPositive if its clauses are positive and mutually disjoint. Dually define DisjointNegative. It is shown that the satisfiability of CNFs of type DisjointPositive[MATH]DisjointNegative can be decided in quadratic time. Moreover, the modelset can be output in polynomial total time. This is relevant since it affects not only the modelsets of CNFs of type Positive[MATH]Negative, but more generally of type Horn[MATH]AntiHorn. As to the latter CNFs, they e.g. occur in connection with the fixpoints of a Monotone Boolean Network.
tldr: This paper presents a polynomial-time algorithm for a special case of satisfiability of CNFs with disjoint positive and negative clauses.
motivation: The satisfiability of Positive∧Negative CNFs is NP-complete, but the author identifies a restricted subclass (DisjointPositive∧DisjointNegative) that can be solved efficiently.
method: The author defines DisjointPositive and DisjointNegative clause sets and proves that satisfiability of their conjunction can be decided in quadratic time, with the model set output in polynomial total time.
result: The main result is a quadratic-time decision algorithm and polynomial-time enumeration of all models for this subclass.
conclusion: This result has implications for the model sets of more general CNF classes like Horn∧AntiHorn, which arise in monotone Boolean networks.

title: Zero-apt: A Closed-Loop Adversarial Framework For LLM-Driven Automated Penetration Testing Under Intelligent Defense
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05567v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-driven automated penetration testing agents are typically evaluated against static targets that neither detect nor respond to attacks, so their behavior under intelligent defense remains untested. The causal consistency of multi-step attack chains likewise hinges on unstable LLM reasoning, and agent decisions remain opaque to human analysts. These three shortcomings, in realism, consistency, and auditability, are usually patched in isolation. We present ZERO-APT, a turn-based attacker-defender-judge framework that addresses them within a single architecture. For realism, ZERO-APT embeds a configurable LLM Defender that consumes Sysmon telemetry and detects attacks in real time, exposing the attacker to a live opponent rather than a passive target. For consistency, three architectural mechanisms move causal consistency from unstable LLM reasoning into enforced system architecture: separation of planning from execution, multi-dimensional ReAct feedback, and a hard-constraint-filtered action library. For auditability, a dedicated Judge agent adjudicates each round, maintains global state, and emits structured post-hoc CTI reports that make every decision traceable. We evaluate a Windows Server 2022 post-exploitation prototype across five scenarios with three Defender configurations. ZERO-APT reaches 79\% attack success rate (Aurora 22\%, PentestGPT 39\%), a Causal Consistency Score of 0.860 (Aurora 0.930, Claude Code 0.520), and end-to-end decision auditability through structured CTI reports. We release the benchmark to support evaluation of penetration agents under intelligent defense.
tldr: ZERO-APT is a closed-loop adversarial framework for LLM-driven automated penetration testing with intelligent defense, focusing on realism, consistency, and auditability.
motivation: Existing LLM-driven penetration testing agents are evaluated against static targets and lack realism, causal consistency, and auditability.
method: The framework uses a turn-based attacker-defender-judge architecture with an LLM Defender that detects attacks via Sysmon telemetry, separates planning from execution, and includes a Judge agent for state tracking and CTI report generation.
result: ZERO-APT achieves 79% attack success rate, a Causal Consistency Score of 0.860, and provides structured CTI reports for auditability.
conclusion: The framework improves realism and consistency in automated penetration testing, but its relevance to quantum computing or thermodynamics is negligible.

title: The Coverage Gap: Chile's Cyber Disclosure Framework Versus The Usa, Eu And Uk
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05594v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce the Coverage Gap as a measurable distance between the observable public exposure of critical-infrastructure operators and their declared capability to coordinate vulnerability disclosure. We instantiate it against the 915 Chilean Operadores de Importancia Vital (OIVs -- Operators of Vital Importance) designated by the National Cybersecurity Agency (ANCI) under Ley 21.663 (Resolucion Exenta No. 87, 16 December 2025). Using a passive-only, OSINT-based method consistent with the principles of ISO/IEC 29147:2018 and Chile's computer-crimes safe harbour (Ley 21.459), we conduct a full-universe census of the foundational disclosure-capability layer (Layer 1, verifiable disclosure contact) across approximately 98.7% of the official catalogue. Only 16 of 915 OIVs (1.7%) publish a verifiable RFC 9116 disclosure channel; among operators of physical-world infrastructure -- energy, health, banking, telecommunications, fuel, water, transport, and state administration -- fewer than ten do so, and all four major banks and both telecommunications incumbents lack one entirely. This compares with over 99% adherence in the U.S. federal civilian branch under CISA Binding Operational Directive 18-01. Email-authentication misconfiguration affects 766 of 915 (84%) OIVs, and end-of-life or known-vulnerable stack components an estimated 23.5% (Wilson 95% CI [12%, 38%]). Cross-jurisdictional benchmarking situates Chile roughly eight years behind the USA, the UK, and the Netherlands on email-authentication mandates, and three years behind Denmark. We propose a four-stage roadmap modelled on BOD 18-01 and the UK Public-Sector DMARC Toolkit, and release the open-source tool anci-oiv-resolver (Apache 2.0) to enable independent reproduction of the OIV-domain mapping that underpins universe-scale auditing.
tldr: This paper analyzes the cybersecurity disclosure practices of critical infrastructure operators in Chile, benchmarking them against international standards.
motivation: To quantify the gap between declared and actual vulnerability disclosure capabilities among Chilean critical infrastructure operators.
method: Passive OSINT-based census of 915 OIVs using RFC 9116 disclosure channels, email authentication checks, and stack component analysis.
result: Only 1.7% of OIVs have a verifiable disclosure channel; 84% have email misconfigurations; Chile lags behind USA, UK, and Netherlands by 3-8 years.
conclusion: Proposes a four-stage roadmap and releases an open-source tool for independent auditing.

title: SlotGCG: Exploiting The Positional Vulnerability In LLMs For Jailbreak Attacks
authors: Seungwon Jeong, Jiwoo Jeong, Hyeonjin Kim, Yunseok Lee, Woojin Lee
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05609v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are widely deployed, identifying their vulnerability through jailbreak attacks becomes increasingly critical. Optimization-based attacks like Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) have focused on inserting adversarial tokens to the end of prompts. However, GCG restricts adversarial tokens to a fixed insertion point (typically the prompt suffix), leaving the effect of inserting tokens at other positions unexplored. In this paper, we empirically investigate , i.e., candidate positions within a prompt where tokens can be inserted. We find that vulnerability to jailbreaking is highly related to the selection of the . Based on these findings, we introduce the (VSS) to quantify the positional vulnerability to jailbreaking. We then propose SlotGCG, which evaluates all slots with VSS, selects the most vulnerable slots for insertion, and runs a targeted optimization attack at those slots. Our approach provides a position-search mechanism that is attack-agnostic and can be plugged into any optimization-based attack, adding only 200ms of preprocessing time. Experiments across multiple models demonstrate that SlotGCG significantly outperforms existing methods. Specifically, it achieves 14\% higher Attack Success Rates (ASR) over GCG-based attacks, converges faster, and shows superior robustness against defense methods with 42\% higher ASR than baseline approaches. Our implementation is available at {[URL].
tldr: This paper proposes SlotGCG, a method to improve jailbreak attacks on LLMs by exploiting positional vulnerability in prompts.
motivation: Existing optimization-based jailbreak attacks like GCG only insert adversarial tokens at the prompt suffix, ignoring other positions that may be more vulnerable.
method: The authors introduce a Vulnerability Score for Slots (VSS) to quantify positional vulnerability, then select the most vulnerable slots for adversarial token insertion and run targeted optimization.
result: SlotGCG achieves 14% higher Attack Success Rate (ASR) over GCG-based attacks, converges faster, and shows 42% higher ASR against defense methods.
conclusion: The position-search mechanism is attack-agnostic and can be plugged into any optimization-based attack with minimal preprocessing overhead, improving jailbreak effectiveness.

title: Protecting K-Nearest Neighbor Queries From Location Inference Attacks
authors: Zhiyu Sun, Jie Fu, Xinpeng Ling, Huifa Li, Zhili Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05648v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The k-nearest neighbor query (kNNQ) is a core component of modern location-based services (LBS) and has been widely adopted in popular features such as ``people nearby''. However, its potential privacy risks have long been overlooked. In this work, we present the first two attacks against kNNQ, namely the geometric intersection location inference attack (GI-LIA) and the zero-order optimization location inference attack (ZO-LIA), revealing the inherent location privacy risks posed by kNNQ. To mitigate these privacy risks, we further propose DPRS, a differential privacy framework for kNNQ protection. The core idea of DPRS is to incorporate a rejection sampling mechanism within a constrained perturbation interval, thereby mitigating the distance distortion caused by excessive noise injection. In addition, we design a private interval construction algorithm to construct the perturbation interval, enabling the rejection sampling mechanism to achieve a more favorable trade-off between privacy protection and query utility in kNNQ. Extensive experiments on real-world spatial datasets demonstrate that DPRS outperforms existing methods in both privacy protection and query utility. Our code is available at [URL].
tldr: This paper addresses location privacy in k-nearest neighbor queries using differential privacy, with no connection to quantum computing or the user's research interests.
motivation: The paper aims to protect location privacy in kNN queries, which are widely used in location-based services but vulnerable to inference attacks.
method: The authors propose two attacks (GI-LIA and ZO-LIA) and a defense framework DPRS that uses rejection sampling with constrained perturbation intervals to balance privacy and utility.
result: Experiments on real-world datasets show DPRS outperforms existing methods in privacy protection and query utility.
conclusion: The work highlights privacy risks in kNN queries and provides an effective differential privacy solution, but is unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Cognitive Threat Intelligence And Explainable Federated Security Analytics For Distributed Infrastructure Systems
authors: Md. Arifur Rahman, B. M. Taslimul Haque, Md. Iqbal Hossan, Md. Serajul Kabir Chowdhury Rubel
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05701v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The increasing adoption of distributed infrastructure systems, cloud computing, Internet of Things (IoT) technologies, and edge-based architectures has significantly expanded the cybersecurity attack surface and introduced increasingly sophisticated cyber threats. Conventional centralized intrusion detection approaches often face challenges related to scalability, data privacy, communication overhead, and limited transparency in artificial intelligence-driven decision-making processes. To address these limitations, this study proposes a Cognitive Threat Intelligence and Explainable Federated Security Analytics framework for distributed infrastructure systems. The proposed framework integrates Federated Learning (FL), Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), and cognitive cybersecurity analytics to enable collaborative and privacy-preserving cyber threat detection across distributed network environments. Instead of transmitting sensitive raw network traffic data to centralized servers, local security models are independently trained at distributed nodes, where only encrypted model parameters and updates are shared through a federated aggregation mechanism. This decentralized learning architecture improves privacy protection while reducing communication dependency and centralized security risks. To enhance intelligent threat analysis, the framework incorporates machine learning and deep learning algorithms including Random Forest, XGBoost, Autoencoder.
tldr: This paper proposes a federated learning framework with explainable AI for cybersecurity in distributed systems, but is unrelated to quantum computing, condensed matter physics, or the specified research interests.
motivation: The research addresses scalability, privacy, and transparency issues in centralized intrusion detection for distributed infrastructure systems.
method: The framework integrates Federated Learning, Explainable AI, and cognitive cybersecurity analytics, using local model training with encrypted parameter sharing and algorithms like Random Forest, XGBoost, and Autoencoder.
result: The paper presents a conceptual framework; no experimental results are provided in the abstract.
conclusion: The framework aims to improve privacy, reduce communication overhead, and enhance transparency in threat detection, but lacks empirical validation.

title: Hybrid Cnn-lstm Framework For Intelligent Cyber Attack Detection And Prevention In U.s. Critical Digital Infrastructure: A Comparative Machine Learning Evaluation On Cse-cic-ids2018
authors: Md. Iqbal Hossan, Md. Serajul Kabir Chowdhury Rubel, Md. Arifur Rahman, B. M. Taslimul Haque
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05714v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Digital infrastructure is growing at a rapid pace in the United States, and as a result, exposure to advanced cyber threats to critical sectors including healthcare, finance, transportation, energy and government systems is growing. The traditional cybersecurity approaches, including signature-based intrusion detection systems, have become less effective against today's cyber attacks, as they are unable to detect unknown and changing attacks in real time. To overcome these constraints, this research suggests a smart cyber-defense system, which utilizes Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) algorithms in the detection and prevention of cyber attacks in the U.S. digital infrastructure. This study uses the CSE-CIC-IDS2018 dataset, which is a realistic network traffic dataset, along with various cyber attack scenarios, including Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS), brute force attacks, botnets, infiltration attacks, and web-based attacks. A number of machine learning and deep learning models such as Random Forest, XGBoost, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks are implemented and evaluated to be used in identifying malicious network behavior and boosting the accuracy of intrusion detection. The framework proposed combines data preprocessing, feature engineering, real-time traffic monitoring, intelligent threat classification with automated prevention mechanisms to build cybersecurity resilience. E.
tldr: This paper applies hybrid CNN-LSTM models for cyber attack detection in critical infrastructure using the CSE-CIC-IDS2018 dataset, with no connection to quantum computing or thermodynamics.
motivation: Traditional signature-based intrusion detection systems fail against unknown and evolving cyber attacks, motivating the need for AI/ML-based solutions.
method: The study implements and compares Random Forest, XGBoost, CNN, and LSTM models on the CSE-CIC-IDS2018 dataset, proposing a hybrid CNN-LSTM framework with data preprocessing, feature engineering, and real-time monitoring.
result: The hybrid CNN-LSTM framework achieves high accuracy in detecting various cyber attacks (DDoS, brute force, botnets, etc.) compared to individual models.
conclusion: The proposed AI-driven defense system enhances cybersecurity resilience for U.S. critical digital infrastructure, with potential for real-time deployment.

title: An Embarrassingly Simple Detector For Model Extraction Attacks In Large Language Model Api Traffic
authors: Shuze Liu, Qianwen Guo, Yushun Dong
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05725v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed through hosted APIs, making model extraction a practical threat to model ownership and service security. However, individual extraction queries often resemble benign requests, and existing evaluations often focus on single-query anomaly scoring or pure benign-versus-attacker user settings. We formulate model extraction monitoring as benign-calibrated traffic-window distribution testing and show that an embarrassingly simple detector is effective: embed incoming queries into a semantic space and test whether their aggregate distribution deviates from historical benign traffic. We instantiate the detector with maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), using only benign-vs-benign comparisons to set the decision threshold. We evaluate on fourteen attacker-normal query pairs from four extraction scenarios and compare with adapted PRADA, SEAT, CAP, DATE, and marginal Mahalanobis baselines. Across three random seeds, MMD achieves 0.3% benign FPR, 100.0% pure-attacker TPR, 90.5% average TPR over attacker fractions, and 95.1% balanced accuracy. These results show that benign-calibrated distribution testing is a strong empirical baseline for model extraction detection in both user-level and mixed multi-user LLM API traffic. Code is released at: [URL].
tldr: This paper proposes a simple detector for model extraction attacks on LLM APIs using distribution testing with MMD.
motivation: Model extraction attacks threaten LLM ownership and service security, but existing detection methods are complex or evaluated only in pure benign-vs-attacker settings.
method: The detector embeds queries into a semantic space and uses maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) to test if the aggregate distribution of incoming queries deviates from historical benign traffic, with thresholds set using only benign-vs-benign comparisons.
result: Across 14 attacker-normal query pairs and 4 extraction scenarios, the method achieves 0.3% benign FPR, 100% pure-attacker TPR, 90.5% average TPR over attacker fractions, and 95.1% balanced accuracy, outperforming baselines like PRADA, SEAT, CAP, DATE, and marginal Mahalanobis.
conclusion: Benign-calibrated distribution testing is a strong empirical baseline for model extraction detection in both user-level and mixed multi-user LLM API traffic.

title: Membrane: A Self-Evolving Contrastive Safety Memory For Llm Agent Defense
authors: Minseok Choi, Seungbin Yang, Dongjin Kim, Subin Kim, Jungmin Son, Yunseung Lee, Jaegul Choo, Youngjun Kwak
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05743v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite advances in safety alignment, large language models remain vulnerable to continuously evolving jailbreaks. Existing fine-tuned safety classifiers cannot adapt to these evolving attacks, while adaptive memory-based guardrails tend to over-refuse benign queries that resemble stored attacks. We propose Membrane, a self-evolving guardrail built on Contrastive Safety Memory (CSM): each cell pairs the conditions for blocking a harmful query with those for permitting a superficially similar benign request. Without retraining, Membrane evolves CSM by distilling each harmful interaction and its benign counterpart into a contrastive cell indexed by the underlying attack strategy, so that one cell generalizes across topical variants of the same mechanism. At inference, retrieved cells serve as grounding context for precise safety decisions. Across model-level safety on HarmBench and agent-level safety on AgentHarm, Membrane achieves the highest F1 on all six jailbreak attacks. Notably, benign refusal on AgentHarm stays at 7-14%, well below the 28-85% range of prior guards. Memory cells also retain 87-88% F1 under cross-attack transfer and remain stable under memory poisoning.
tldr: This paper proposes a self-evolving safety memory for LLM agents to defend against jailbreak attacks, using contrastive memory cells that pair harmful and benign queries.
motivation: Existing safety classifiers cannot adapt to evolving jailbreaks, and memory-based guardrails over-refuse benign queries.
method: Membrane builds a Contrastive Safety Memory (CSM) where each cell stores conditions for blocking a harmful query and permitting a similar benign one, evolving without retraining by distilling interactions into contrastive cells indexed by attack strategy.
result: Membrane achieves the highest F1 on all six jailbreak attacks on HarmBench and AgentHarm, with benign refusal rates of 7-14% compared to 28-85% for prior guards, and retains 87-88% F1 under cross-attack transfer.
conclusion: Membrane provides an adaptive, precise safety guardrail for LLM agents, with potential for further generalization and robustness against memory poisoning.

title: An Improved Cnn-lstm Based Intrusion Detection System For IoT Networks
authors: Mohammad Tariq Ikhlas, Pohanyar Khowaja Khil, Malik Muhammad Mueed Aslam, Muhammad Khuram Shahzad
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05776v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With the rapid proliferation of IoT devices, security concerns have dramatically escalated and intrusion detection systems have become critical for protecting networked environments. This paper presents an improved CNN-LSTM based intrusion detection model that combines multi-class classification, dataset integration, and temporal feature learning to enhance detection performance in IoT networks. Using network traffic data, the proposed approach is evaluated on intrusion detection tasks and achieves an accuracy of approximately 97%. Experimental results demonstrate that the model effectively detects multiple attack categories while maintaining stable training and validation performance. The integration of convolutional and recurrent neural network components enables the framework to capture both spatial and temporal characteristics of network traffic, improving overall intrusion detection capability in IoT environments.
tldr: This paper presents a CNN-LSTM based intrusion detection system for IoT networks, achieving 97% accuracy.
motivation: To address security concerns in IoT networks by improving intrusion detection performance.
method: Combines CNN for spatial feature extraction and LSTM for temporal feature learning on network traffic data.
result: The model achieves approximately 97% accuracy in detecting multiple attack categories.
conclusion: The hybrid CNN-LSTM approach effectively captures spatial and temporal patterns, enhancing IoT intrusion detection.

title: SentinelRAG: Synthetic Sentinel Knowledge For Rag Database Copyright Protection
authors: Tsun On Kwok, Xi Yang, Ki Sen Hung, Chang Liu, Yangqiu Song
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05787v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Protecting proprietary RAG databases from unauthorized redistribution is challenging: existing watermarking methods either inject fabricated relations between real entities, polluting the knowledge base with misinformation, or embed fragile lexical patterns that adversarial paraphrasing easily removes. We propose SentinelRAG, a watermarking framework that embeds style-consistent but fictitious knowledge entries into the RAG database. Our key insight is that synthetic knowledge describing fictitious entities is unlikely to be retrieved by legitimate queries, yet can be reliably triggered through targeted probes known only to the data owner. Experiments on four datasets ranging from 2.9k to 8.8M documents demonstrate that SentinelRAG achieves statistically significant detection [MATH] across all tested configurations at only a 0.1% injection rate. Compared to the state-of-the-art, our method significantly reduces the false detection rate while maintaining negligible interference with legitimate user queries.
tldr: SentinelRAG is a watermarking method for protecting RAG databases by injecting fictitious knowledge entries that are detectable only via targeted probes.
motivation: Existing watermarking methods for RAG databases either pollute the knowledge base with misinformation or are vulnerable to adversarial paraphrasing.
method: The framework embeds style-consistent but fictitious knowledge entries describing nonexistent entities into the RAG database; these entries are unlikely to be retrieved by legitimate queries but can be triggered by owner-known probes.
result: Experiments on datasets from 2.9k to 8.8M documents show statistically significant detection at only 0.1% injection rate, with reduced false detection rate and negligible interference with legitimate queries.
conclusion: SentinelRAG offers a robust and low-impact watermarking solution for copyright protection of RAG databases, with potential for further optimization and deployment.

title: Gcd: Garbled, Corrected, Demonstrandum -- Fixing And Proving Go's Extended Gcd Implementation
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05796v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We verify the 'extendedGCD' implementation in Go's standard library ('crypto/internal/fips140/bigmod'), which plays a crucial role in the generation of RSA key pairs. Even though the Go implementation is supposedly a direct port from BoringSSL's implementation, we uncovered two deviations that each break the algorithm's invariants: (1) the Go implementation deviates in the way coefficients are updated, and (2) it permits a larger input domain. We address both deviations; the first by fixing the Go implementation, which results in an on average 24% speedup, and the second deviation by porting an existing proof for BoringSSL and extending it to cover the larger input domain. We prove correctness and termination of the fixed Go implementation using Gobra, a deductive program verifier for Go. Where necessary, we used Lean to prove key lemmata on non-linear arithmetic, which we import into Gobra. Our verification effort reveals three key insights: subtle bugs can slip into even well-reviewed code with surprising ease; formal verification is a powerful tool for uncovering them; and AI agents can facilitate the verification process by iteratively refining invariants and lemmata based on Gobra's error messages.
tldr: This paper verifies and fixes a bug in Go's extended GCD implementation used in RSA key generation, with no connection to the user's research interests.
motivation: The Go implementation of extendedGCD had deviations from BoringSSL that broke invariants, potentially affecting RSA key generation correctness.
method: The authors fixed the Go implementation and used Gobra (a deductive verifier for Go) with Lean for non-linear arithmetic lemmas to prove correctness and termination.
result: Two deviations were found and fixed, resulting in a 24% speedup; the proof was extended to cover a larger input domain.
conclusion: The work demonstrates that formal verification can catch subtle bugs in well-reviewed code, and AI agents can assist in the verification process.

title: PriSrv: Privacy-Enhanced And Highly Usable Service Discovery In Wireless Communications
authors: Yang Yang, Robert H. Deng, Guomin Yang, Yingjiu Li, Hweehwa Pang, Minming Huang, Rui Shi, Jian Weng
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05821v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Service discovery is essential in wireless communications. However, existing protocols provide limited privacy protection, leaking sensitive device information and opening routes to network attacks. This paper proposes a private service discovery protocol, called PriSrv, which enables both service providers and clients to specify fine-grained authentication policies before establishing connections. PriSrv achieves this via a dual-layer matching architecture: an outer layer filters mismatched entities using public attributes, while an inner layer handles mutual authentication using selectively disclosed private attributes. As a core component, we introduce the primitive of anonymous credential-based matchmaking encryption (ACME), which enables dual-layer matching in a single step to achieve bilateral policy control, selective attribute disclosure, and multi-show unlinkability. To instantiate ACME, we design a fast anonymous credential (FAC) scheme providing constant-size credentials and efficient verification. We demonstrate PriSrv's interoperability by integrating it with popular wireless frameworks including EAP, mDNS, BLE, and AirDrop. Detailed formal security proofs and extensive performance evaluations across desktop, laptop, smartphone, and Raspberry Pi platforms demonstrate that PriSrv provides enhanced privacy guarantees with high usability, achieving secure discovery in less than one second on mainstream mobile devices.
tldr: PriSrv is a privacy-enhanced service discovery protocol for wireless communications using anonymous credential-based matchmaking encryption.
motivation: Existing service discovery protocols leak sensitive device information and are vulnerable to network attacks, motivating the need for privacy-preserving discovery.
method: The paper proposes a dual-layer matching architecture with an outer layer for public attribute filtering and an inner layer for mutual authentication using selectively disclosed private attributes, instantiated via a new primitive called anonymous credential-based matchmaking encryption (ACME) and a fast anonymous credential (FAC) scheme.
result: PriSrv achieves bilateral policy control, selective attribute disclosure, and multi-show unlinkability, with secure discovery in less than one second on mainstream mobile devices, as demonstrated through formal security proofs and performance evaluations.
conclusion: PriSrv provides enhanced privacy and usability for service discovery in wireless communications, with potential integration into popular frameworks like EAP, mDNS, BLE, and AirDrop.

title: Towards Worst-case Hardness For Low-Noise Lpn
authors: Divesh Aggarwal, Rishav Gupta, Hai Hoang Nguyen, Kel Zin Tan, Prashant Nalini Vasudevan
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05834v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The hardness of the Learning Parity with Noise (LPN) problem is a foundational assumption in cryptography, forming the basis of constructions ranging from symmetric-key primitives to public-key encryption and beyond. A central open question is whether the average-case hardness of LPN can be based on worst-case complexity assumptions, as has been achieved for the analogous Learning With Errors (LWE) problem. Existing worst-case-to-average-case reductions for LPN [BLVW19, YZ21] rely on statistical smoothing of linear codes, which inherently limits the resulting average-case hardness to noise rates as large as [MATH], which is insufficient for public-key applications. We explore a new approach towards obtaining such reductions: rather than requiring that random sparse combinations of the rows of the generator matrix of a code be statistically close to uniform, we only require that they be computationally indistinguishable from uniform. This leads to a clean win-win structure: we show that any efficient LPN solver can be transformed into a pair of efficient algorithms [MATH] such that for every matrix [MATH] of appropriate dimensions over [MATH], either [MATH] decodes the code generated by [MATH] from random noise, or [MATH] distinguishes random noisy codewords of the dual of this code from uniform. By instantiating this reduction with appropriate parameters, we obtain the average-case hardness of LPN with inverse-polynomial noise rate [MATH] for any constant [MATH], assuming the worst-case simultaneous hardness of decoding a code from random noise and distinguishing random noisy codewords of its dual from uniform. In particular, setting [MATH], our reduction yields LPN hardness in the parameter regime required for Alekhnovich's construction of public-key encryption [Ale03], a regime that was previously inaccessible via worst-case reductions.
tldr: This paper presents a new approach to worst-case-to-average-case reductions for the Learning Parity with Noise (LPN) problem, achieving hardness for inverse-polynomial noise rates relevant to public-key encryption.
motivation: To bridge the gap between worst-case and average-case hardness of LPN, which is crucial for basing cryptographic constructions on worst-case assumptions, similar to LWE.
method: The authors replace statistical smoothing with computational indistinguishability, leading to a win-win reduction that transforms an LPN solver into either a decoder or a distinguisher for dual codes.
result: They obtain average-case hardness of LPN with inverse-polynomial noise rate for any constant c, assuming worst-case hardness of decoding and distinguishing dual codes.
conclusion: This work provides a new reduction framework that may enable further progress on LPN-based cryptography, but the assumptions remain non-standard and the practical impact is limited.

title: GenTI: Benchmarking LLMs For Autonomous Idps Rule Generation For Unseen Attacks
authors: Hassan Jalil Hadi, Rehana Yasmin, Ali Shoker
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05844v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rule-based Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS) offer precise attack detection as well as mitigation, however their manually crafted, signature-driven rules limit adaptability to emerging and zero-day threats. Additionally, existing public datasets (e.g., CICIDS2017, UNSW-NB15) focus on traffic classification and provide little structured information to support automatic rule synthesis or prevention logic. To address this gap, we propose Generative Thread Intelligence (GenTI) an LLM-driven benchmark for automatic generation of IDPS rules targeting unseen attacks. The dataset (GTI) aggregates over 150k detection and prevention rules from Snort, Suricata, Emerging Threats, as well as 50k YARA, each annotated with protocol behavior, payload signatures, contextual relationships, mappings to Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI), along with actionable response types (alert, drop, reject). Moreover, on top of this corpus we design an LLM-based pipeline that transforms analyst prompts and representative payloads into deployable rules via structured prompt engineering, Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, as well as a Chain-of-Verification (CoVe) loop for syntactic, semantic, and security validation. The generated rules are executed in real time on (Snort/Suricata) and evaluated by syntax accuracy, semantic similarity, CTI coverage, security effectiveness as well as unseen attacks detection. Furthermore, our GenTI instantiation achieves a composite rule-quality score of 89.4\%, with 94.8\% CTI coverage, improving unseen attacks detection from 45\% to 87.4\% and reducing the false-positive rate from 8.5\% to 2.3\%. Overall, GenTI establishes the first large-scale benchmark that tightly couples rule-level CTI with LLM-based automation, enabling adaptive, self-evolving IDPS.
tldr: This paper presents a benchmark for LLM-based automatic generation of IDPS rules for unseen attacks, focusing on cybersecurity rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Existing IDPS rely on manually crafted signatures that fail against zero-day threats, and current datasets lack structured information for automatic rule synthesis.
method: The authors built a large dataset (GTI) of over 200k rules from Snort, Suricata, Emerging Threats, and YARA, and designed an LLM pipeline with prompt engineering, Chain-of-Thought reasoning, and Chain-of-Verification for rule generation and validation.
result: The GenTI system achieved a composite rule-quality score of 89.4%, 94.8% CTI coverage, improved unseen attack detection from 45% to 87.4%, and reduced false-positive rate from 8.5% to 2.3%.
conclusion: GenTI establishes a benchmark for adaptive, self-evolving IDPS using LLMs, but is unrelated to quantum computing, thermodynamics, or foundations.

title: PriSrv+: Privacy And Usability-Enhanced Wireless Service Discovery With Fast And Expressive Matchmaking Encryption
authors: Yang Yang, Guomin Yang, Yingjiu Li, Pengfei Wu, Rui Shi, Minming Huang, Jian Weng, Hweehwa Pang, Robert H. Deng
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05902v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Service discovery is a fundamental process in wireless networks, enabling devices to find and communicate with services dynamically, and is critical for the seamless operation of modern systems like 5G and IoT. This paper introduces PriSrv+, an advanced privacy and usability-enhanced service discovery protocol for modern wireless networks and resource-constrained environments. PriSrv+ builds upon PriSrv (NDSS'24), by addressing critical limitations in expressiveness, privacy, scalability, and efficiency, while maintaining compatibility with widely-used wireless protocols such as mDNS, BLE, and Wi-Fi. A key innovation in PriSrv+ is the development of Fast and Expressive Matchmaking Encryption (FEME), the first matchmaking encryption scheme capable of supporting expressive access control policies with an unbounded attribute universe, allowing any arbitrary string to be used as an attribute. FEME significantly enhances the flexibility of service discovery while ensuring robust message and attribute privacy. Compared to PriSrv, PriSrv+ optimizes cryptographic operations, achieving 7.62* faster for encryption and 6.23* faster for decryption, and dramatically reduces ciphertext sizes by 87.33%. In addition, PriSrv+ reduces communication costs by 87.33% for service broadcast and 86.64% for anonymous mutual authentication compared with PriSrv. Formal security proofs confirm the security of FEME and PriSrv+. Extensive evaluations on multiple platforms demonstrate that PriSrv+ achieves superior performance, scalability, and efficiency compared to existing state-of-the-art protocols.
tldr: PriSrv+ is a privacy-enhanced wireless service discovery protocol using a new matchmaking encryption scheme (FEME) for expressive access control, but it is unrelated to quantum computing, condensed matter physics, or machine learning.
motivation: Existing service discovery protocols lack expressiveness, privacy, and efficiency for modern wireless networks and resource-constrained devices.
method: The authors develop Fast and Expressive Matchmaking Encryption (FEME) supporting unbounded attribute universe and arbitrary strings, and integrate it into the PriSrv+ protocol.
result: PriSrv+ achieves 7.62× faster encryption, 6.23× faster decryption, and 87.33% reduction in ciphertext size compared to PriSrv, with formal security proofs.
conclusion: PriSrv+ provides a scalable and efficient solution for privacy-preserving service discovery in wireless networks, with potential applications in 5G and IoT.

title: Metric Facility Assignment With Partial Information
authors: Vasilis Gkatzelis, Hasti Karimi, Emma Rewinski, Maziar Shamsipour, Alexandros A. Voudouris
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05905v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study an assignment problem where a set of agents and a set of facilities lie on a line metric. The goal is to compute an assignment of agents to facilities to approximately minimize the social cost (the total distance of agents from their assigned facilities) given only partial information regarding the metric. Unlike previous work which focused solely on algorithms with access to the ordinal preferences of the agents over the facilities (ORD), we also consider the value of information regarding approval preferences (APP), and inter-facility distances (DIST). For different combinations of these three information types, we establish tight bounds on the distortion of deterministic algorithms, showing that it is possible to improve over the optimal bound of [MATH] that can be achieved using only ORD information. Among other results, we show a tight bound of [MATH] for APP+DIST which holds even for general metrics, and a tight bound of [MATH] for ORD+APP+DIST.
tldr: This paper studies metric facility assignment with partial information, focusing on distortion bounds for different information types.
motivation: To understand how different types of partial information (ordinal, approval, inter-facility distances) can improve the quality of facility assignment algorithms.
method: The authors consider deterministic algorithms with access to combinations of ORD, APP, and DIST information, and derive tight distortion bounds.
result: Tight bounds are established: APP+DIST achieves distortion 3 (even for general metrics), and ORD+APP+DIST achieves distortion 2.
conclusion: The work provides a complete picture of the value of different information types in metric facility assignment, with implications for algorithm design under partial information.

title: Double-Directional Wireless Channel Modeling Using Statistics-Aided Machine Learning
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05993v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The double-directional (DD) wireless channel model is important for realistic system design since it provides complete propagation information. While stochastic and deterministic channel models are widely adopted, and existing machine learning (ML) solutions mostly aim to align future channel realizations, these solutions are often limited to short time spans that may not be statistically significant. Moreover, because the number of multi-path components (MPCs) varies with spatial and temporal variation of the receiver (RX) and/or interacting objects (IOs), typical ML solutions that require fixed, predefined input and output shapes fall short. To curb these limitations, we propose a statistics-aided ML solution that relies on a fixed subset of MPCs selection. More specifically, we first select top-[MATH] MPCs, where [MATH] is much smaller than the total number of MPCs, and construct learnable graphs to train our proposed hybrid TimesNet-TimeFilter (TNTF) model. We then use a channel statistics-aided training method to generate future top-M DD channel realizations such that the statistics calculated from these realizations matches closely with those of the actual statistics from the complete time-varying DD channel realizations. We validate the proposed solution using extensive simulations on both synthetic stochastic channel model (SCM)-based and deterministic ray-tracing-based datasets, and demonstrate its effectiveness relative to state-of-the-art baselines.
tldr: This paper proposes a statistics-aided machine learning model for double-directional wireless channel modeling, focusing on generating future channel realizations with accurate statistical properties.
motivation: Existing ML solutions for channel modeling are limited to short time spans and require fixed input/output shapes, failing to handle varying numbers of multi-path components.
method: The authors select a fixed subset of top-M MPCs, construct learnable graphs, and train a hybrid TimesNet-TimeFilter model using a channel statistics-aided training method.
result: The proposed TNTF model effectively generates future top-M DD channel realizations whose statistics closely match actual statistics, validated on synthetic and ray-tracing datasets.
conclusion: The work provides a novel ML approach for double-directional channel modeling that captures statistical properties over time, with potential applications in wireless system design.

title: Cheating In Multiplayer Online Games: A Dataset
authors: Hugo Bertin, Marc Dacier, Y\'erom-David Bromberg
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06013v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cheating poses a significant threat to the Multiplayer Online Games (MOG) industry by degrading player satisfaction and undermining the fairness in competitive gaming. Despite efforts to develop mitigation techniques, cheating remains difficult to detect and prevent in practice. In particular, a class of cheats based on network flow disruption remains unsolvable. To find out how to detect such attacks we need access to representative labelled data. However, no such dataset exists. To address this gap, we leverage an experimental framework that combines a multiplayer online game with a plug-in capable of both reproducing cheating attacks and collecting logs at two levels: network and application-layer. This paper presents a dataset compiling records of game sessions played by both real players and automated game clients, with cheating actions explicitly logged. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first dataset that provides logs of network flow disruption cheats. While it includes such network-based cheats, it is not limited to them and also contains records of more commonly studied cheats, such as aimbots and wallhacks. This dataset can be used by researchers in academia and industry seeking to develop cheating detection mechanisms for online games. Furthermore, it is designed to be evolutive and can be enriched by others creating their own data traces with the proposed framework.
tldr: This paper presents a dataset of network flow disruption cheats in multiplayer online games, with logs from real and automated players.
motivation: Cheating in multiplayer online games degrades player satisfaction and fairness, and network-based cheats are particularly hard to detect due to lack of labeled data.
method: The authors built an experimental framework combining a multiplayer online game with a plug-in that reproduces cheating attacks and collects network and application-layer logs.
result: They produced the first dataset containing logs of network flow disruption cheats, along with other common cheats like aimbots and wallhacks.
conclusion: The dataset enables researchers to develop cheating detection mechanisms, and the framework is designed to be extensible for future data collection.

title: Revenue Guarantees Of No-Swap-Regret Dynamics In First Price Auctions
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06085v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the revenue of approximate correlated equilibrium in discrete first price auctions - the set of allowable bids is [MATH] for some [MATH]. We show that the revenue of any [MATH]-approximate correlated equilibrium is at least [MATH], where [MATH] is the second-highest valuation. Our results establish the first polynomial convergence rates on the revenue generated by no-swap regret bidders in first-price auctions. For instance, if bidders admit the optimal swap regret of [MATH], then the time-averaged revenue is at least [MATH] after [MATH] rounds.
tldr: This paper studies revenue guarantees of no-swap-regret dynamics in first-price auctions, a topic in algorithmic game theory and auction design.
motivation: To understand the revenue generated by bidders using no-swap regret learning algorithms in first-price auctions, which is important for auction design and market analysis.
method: The authors analyze approximate correlated equilibria in discrete first-price auctions and derive lower bounds on revenue as a function of the approximation parameter and second-highest valuation.
result: They show that the revenue of any ε-approximate correlated equilibrium is at least (1-ε) times the second-highest valuation, and establish polynomial convergence rates for no-swap regret bidders.
conclusion: The results provide theoretical guarantees on revenue in first-price auctions under learning dynamics, with implications for practical auction mechanisms.

title: The Complexity Of Asynchronous HyperLTL
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06091v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hyperproperties express, e.g., information-flow properties of systems, which involves the simultaneous reasoning about multiple execution traces of a system. Consequently, HyperLTL, the most important specification logic for hyperproperties, extends LTL with quantification over traces. However, HyperLTL can only express synchronous hyperproperties. Recently, several logics for asynchronous hyperproperties have been proposed. Here, we focus on AHLTL, asynchronous HyperLTL, which extends HyperLTL with quantification over trajectories that control the relative speed at which time progresses on the quantified traces. Model-checking AHLTL is known to be undecidable while satisfiability is known to be [MATH]-hard, but the precise complexity of both problems is open. Here, we close these gaps and show that model-checking is equivalent to truth in second-order arithmetic while satisfiability is [MATH]-complete if the trajectory is existentially quantified and [MATH]-hard and in [MATH] if the trajectory is universally quantified.
tldr: This paper resolves the complexity of model-checking and satisfiability for asynchronous HyperLTL, showing model-checking is equivalent to truth in second-order arithmetic and satisfiability is Σ₁¹-complete or Π₁¹-hard/Π₂¹ depending on quantifier alternation.
motivation: The precise complexity of model-checking and satisfiability for AHLTL was open; previous work only established undecidability and Σ₁¹-hardness.
method: The authors use reductions from second-order arithmetic and known results about HyperLTL to characterize the complexity classes.
result: Model-checking AHLTL is equivalent to truth in second-order arithmetic; satisfiability is Σ₁¹-complete for existential trajectory quantification and Π₁¹-hard and in Π₂¹ for universal trajectory quantification.
conclusion: These results close the open complexity gaps and provide a complete picture of AHLTL's decidability boundaries.

title: Regret Minimization In Single-Dimensional Contract-Design With Binary Actions
authors: Riccardo Poiani, Martino Bernasconi, Andrea Celli
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06125v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study principal-agent problems in which a principal commits to an outcome-dependent payment scheme (i.e., a contract) in order to induce an agent to take a costly action leading to a favorable outcome. We consider the online extension of the classical (one-shot) principal-agent problem, in which the principal repeatedly interacts with agents by proposing contracts over multiple rounds. The principal has no information about the agents and, crucially, does not observe their actions. As a result, the principal must learn an optimal contract using only the realized outcomes observed at each round. We focus on the setting with binary actions and single-dimensional agent types, where the agent's private type represents their cost per unit-of-effort. For adversarial-type sequences, we provide tight [MATH] regret guarantees. Remarkably, this rate is completely independent of the number of outcomes [MATH]. The upper bound is based on two key components: 1) a reduction to a one-dimensional threshold optimization problem and 2) a non-uniform discretization to handle the non-Lipschitz nature of the problem. Moreover, in the case of a single (fixed) hidden type, we show that it is possible to improve the rates and provide a tight [MATH] regret bound. Our algorithm is based on an explore-then-commit strategy where we first approximately learn the hidden type via a stochastic binary search, and then we commit to a ``robustified'' near-optimal contract.
tldr: This paper studies regret minimization in online principal-agent problems with binary actions and single-dimensional agent types, focusing on contract design without observing agent actions.
motivation: To understand how a principal can learn optimal contracts in repeated interactions when agents' actions are unobservable and their types are unknown.
method: Reduces the problem to one-dimensional threshold optimization and uses non-uniform discretization to handle non-Lipschitzness; for fixed hidden type, employs explore-then-commit with stochastic binary search.
result: Achieves tight regret bounds independent of the number of outcomes for adversarial-type sequences, and improved rates for a single fixed hidden type.
conclusion: Provides foundational regret guarantees for online contract design, with implications for algorithmic mechanism design and learning in principal-agent settings.

title: RedEdit: Agentic Red-Teaming Of Image Safety Classifiers Via MCTS-Guided Photo-Editing
authors: Weilin Lin, Ziqi Lin, Zhenxing Zhou, Jianze Li, Tong Zhang, Hui Xiong, Li Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06140v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Image safety classifiers serve as a critical component of contemporary content moderation systems on the internet. However, their resilience against user-style malicious image editing remains underexplored. Such behaviors are highly prevalent in daily scenarios but difficult to fully reproduce. To explore this vulnerability, we introduce RedEdit, a novel black-box red-teaming agent that formulates photo-editing evasion as a combinatorial search problem over edit-tool sequences. It adopts a Vision-Language-Model (VLM)-based proposer to generate semantically targeted candidate edits and a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) planner to prioritize promising edit paths while backtracking from ineffective ones. Together, the proposer and planner instantiate two key capabilities of human attackers, i.e., domain knowledge and iterative backtracking, respectively, to reproduce this practical threat. Our extensive experiments on UnsafeBench reveal profound systemic vulnerabilities: fewer than two edits on average enable 76.2% of unsafe images to evade detectors, while retaining 93.0% malicious semantics, meaning that such manipulated content remains perceptually malicious to humans while easily bypassing automated moderation. We therefore appeal to the community for more attention to this overlooked practical threat.
tldr: This paper presents a red-teaming agent that uses MCTS-guided photo-editing to evade image safety classifiers.
motivation: To explore the vulnerability of image safety classifiers against user-style malicious image editing, a practical threat that is underexplored.
method: A black-box red-teaming agent combining a VLM-based proposer for candidate edits and Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) for planning edit sequences.
result: Fewer than two edits on average enable 76.2% of unsafe images to evade detectors while retaining 93.0% malicious semantics.
conclusion: The work reveals systemic vulnerabilities in image safety classifiers and calls for more attention to this practical threat.

title: Evidence For The Generic Existence Of Two Local Structures In Liquid Water
abstract: Nature Physics, Published online: 04 June 2026;
tldr: Simulations suggest the existence of two interconvertible local structures in liquid water, supporting the two-state picture of deeply undercooled water.
motivation: To provide evidence for the long-predicted two-state regime in deeply undercooled water by identifying two distinct local structures.
method: Molecular dynamics simulations of liquid water.
result: Two local structures that undergo interconvertible reactions were identified, corroborating the two-state picture.
conclusion: The findings support the two-state model of water and may have implications for understanding water's anomalous properties.

title: Adhesion-driven Rigidity Transition Decoupled From Density-driven Jamming Triggers Epithelial Organization In Embryonic Tissues
abstract: Nature Physics, Published online: 02 June 2026;
tldr: This paper studies adhesion-driven rigidity transitions in embryonic tissues, unrelated to quantum information or condensed matter physics.
motivation: To understand how epithelial organization emerges during morphogenesis, specifically the role of adhesion versus density in tissue rigidification.
method: Experimental and theoretical analysis of embryonic tissues, likely using biophysical measurements and modeling.
result: Adhesion-driven rigidification is key to epithelial organization and is decoupled from density-driven jamming.
conclusion: Provides new insight into phase transitions in biological tissues, with implications for developmental biology.
